b-j-habibie: Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie was born on 25 June 1936 in Parepare, South Sulawesi, the son of Alwi Abdul Jalil Habibie, an agriculturist of Bugis-Gorontalese descent, and R. A. Tuti Marini Puspowardojo, a Javanese noblewoman from Yogyakarta. He began to study aviation at Delft in the Netherlands but, because of the dispute between the two countries over West New Guinea, moved to the Technische Hochschule Aachen in Germany, where he took an engineer's degree in 1960 and a doctorate in aerospace engineering in 1965. In 1962 he married Hasri Ainun Besari, a medical doctor.

He joined Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm in Hamburg, where he worked on the Airbus A-300B and reached a middle management post in 1974. That year President Suharto recruited him to return as part of a drive to industrialise Indonesia. Two years later he became head of the new state aircraft maker, known as IPTN, which built Puma helicopters and CASA planes and in 1995 produced a small passenger aircraft, the N-250, a commercial failure.

From 1978 he was state minister of research and technology. By 1991 he oversaw ten state-owned industries, among them shipbuilding, steel, arms and energy; an estimate of 1993 put their cost at nearly 2 billion dollars a year in state funds. In 1990 he was elected the first chair of the Indonesian Association of Muslim Intellectuals, a modernist organisation that gave him a political base. When Suharto signalled in January 1998, during the Asian financial crisis, that he wanted him as vice-president, the rupiah fell.

As president he also forbade the official use of the terms pribumi and non-pribumi, lifted restrictions on the teaching of Mandarin Chinese and passed laws giving autonomy to regencies and cities. He had opposed independence for East Timor and offered special autonomy; the armed forces' leaders were not consulted on his decision to hold a referendum. After the vote of 30 August 1999 pro-Indonesian militias killed and displaced large numbers of people, and on 12 September he accepted a peacekeeping force mandated by the United Nations.

A leaked telephone call with his attorney general raised doubts about the investigation of Suharto. The Bank Bali scandal of 1999, in which bank funds reached members of his re-election team, damaged him further. In October 1999 the assembly known as the MPR rejected his accountability speech by 355 votes to 322, and he withdrew his candidacy; Abdurrahman Wahid succeeded him. He died in the Gatot Soebroto Army Hospital on 11 September 2019 and was buried at the Kalibata Heroes' Cemetery beside his wife.
baghdad: Baghdad stands on a vast, almost entirely flat and low-lying plain bisected by the Tigris, formed by the periodic flooding of the river. The river divides the city into an eastern half, Risafa, and a western half, Karkh. The Diyala river, a tributary of the Tigris, flows south-east of the city and borders its eastern suburbs.

After the fall of the Umayyads the victorious Abbasids sought a new capital. On 30 July 762 the Caliph al-Mansur commissioned the construction of Baghdad, guided by the Iranian Barmakids, believing the site ideal for ruling the Islamic Empire. He hired two designers, Naubakht, a Zoroastrian, and Mashallah, a Jew from Khorasan, who chose an auspicious founding date under the sign of Leo. The historian al-Tabari recorded a prophecy of Christian monks about a leader named Miklas who would build a great city there, and al-Mansur, once called Miklas, saw it as a good omen.

Baghdad became the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate and an intellectual and cultural centre, with institutions such as the House of Wisdom and a multi-ethnic, multi-religious population. For much of the Abbasid era, the Islamic Golden Age, it was one of the largest cities in the world, and its population peaked at more than a million. The Round City, its original core, ceased to exist as a result of the Mongol siege. The Mongol Empire largely destroyed Baghdad in 1258, and a long decline followed, marked by frequent plagues and shifts of power between successive empires.

Later Baghdad was the administrative centre of Ottoman Iraq, with authority over the provinces of Basra, Mosul and Shahrizor. During the First World War it was made the capital of Mandatory Iraq. After Iraq was recognised as an independent monarchy in 1932 the city gradually regained some of its prominence as a centre of Arab culture. It suffered severe damage in the Iraq War, which began with the invasion of 2003, and lost much cultural heritage and many historical artifacts.

Baghdad is the capital and largest city of Iraq and its seat of government, on the banks of the Tigris. Its estimated population is 8 million. Historic mosques, churches, mandis and synagogues reflect its diversity, and the Masjid al-Kadhimayn, the Buratha Mosque, the Shrine of Abdul-Qadir Gilani and the Abu Hanifa Mosque are visited by millions each year. The University of Baghdad is the largest university in Iraq, and the city joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network as a City of Literature in December 2015.
bahadur-shah-of-gujarat: Born Bahadur Khan into the Muzaffarid dynasty, he was the son of Prince Khalil Khan, who became sultan in 1511 as Muzaffar Shah II, and of Rani Lakshmi Bai, daughter of a Gohel Rajput. His grandfather, Sultan Mahmud Begada, kept him at court. When his elder brother Sikandar Shah was named heir, Bahadur Khan feared for his life and fled, first to Chittor and then to Ibrahim Lodi; he was present at the Battle of Panipat without taking part in the fighting.

Muzaffar Shah II died in 1526. Sikandar Shah was murdered after a few weeks on the instructions of his slave Imad-ul-Mulk Khush Kadam, who put an infant brother on the throne as Mahmud Shah II. Bahadur Khan returned, the nobles joined him, and he marched on Champaner, executed Imad-ul-Mulk and had the child poisoned.

Bahadur Shah campaigned in the Deccan in 1528 and 1529, taking the fort of Ahmednagar and forcing the rulers of Ahmadnagar and Berar to sign a humiliating treaty. The fortress of Mandu fell on 28 March 1531, when Sultan Mahmud Shah II of Malwa and his seven sons were captured; they were later put to death by their guards during a rescue attempt. In 1532 he raised a siege of Chittor in return for an enormous ransom. Until his defeat by Humayun the power of Gujarat was at its height, with the rulers of Ahmednagar and Burhanpur acknowledging him as overlord.

The quarrel with Humayun began because Bahadur Shah had sheltered the Mughal prince Muhammad Zaman Mirza. The rout near Mandasur is usually explained by the treachery of Rumi Khan, the Turkish head of the Gujarat artillery. Bahadur Shah fled to Mandu, Champaner and finally Diu. When Humayun left to face the revolt of Sher Shah Suri, the country rose, and Bahadur Shah defeated the Mughals at Kanij and expelled them from Gujarat.

The Treaty of Bassein was signed on 23 December 1534 aboard the galleon St. Mattheus. Having recovered his kingdom, Bahadur Shah regretted the alliance. In February 1537 he visited the Portuguese viceroy's ship off Diu and was attacked and killed on his way back, on 13 February; his body was thrown into the sea. According to the Mirat-i-Sikandari, the viceroy had intercepted his message inviting the Deccan sultans to ally against the Portuguese. He left no son, and after his chosen heir, his nephew Miran Muhammad Shah of Khandesh, died on the way to Gujarat, the nobles chose Mahmud Shah III, son of his brother Latif Khan.
bahrain: Bahrain is a generally flat and arid archipelago in the Persian Gulf, lying between Qatar and the northeastern coast of Saudi Arabia. A low desert plain rises gently to a low central escarpment, whose highest point is the 134 metre Mountain of Smoke (Jabal ad Dukhan). About 92 per cent of the country is desert, with periodic droughts and dust storms. Land reclamation has enlarged the area from 665 to 780 square kilometres, and by August 2008 the number of islands and island groups had risen from 33 to 84.

The name Bahrain is the dual form of the Arabic word bahr, 'sea', so al-Bahrayn originally means 'the two seas'. Which two seas is disputed: the bay east and west of the island, the seas north and south of it, and the salt and fresh water above and below the ground have all been proposed. The term appears five times in the Quran but does not refer to the modern island, which the Arabs originally called Awal. Until the late Middle Ages 'Bahrain' meant a region of Eastern Arabia stretching from Basra in Iraq to the Strait of Hormuz.

Bahrain was home to Dilmun, a Bronze Age trade centre linking Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, and was later ruled by the Sumerians and Babylonians. From the 6th to the 3rd century BCE it was part of the Achaemenid Empire. By about 250 BCE Parthia had brought the Persian Gulf under its control, and it established garrisons along the southern coast of the Gulf to control trade routes.

The ancient Greeks called the island Tylos and knew it as a centre of pearl trading. The admiral Nearchus, serving under Alexander the Great, is believed to have been the first of Alexander's commanders to visit it. He recorded large plantations of cotton trees on Tylos, from which cloth called sindones was made. Bahrain became part of the Hellenised world: the language of the upper classes was Greek, with Aramaic in everyday use, and local coinage shows a seated Zeus, who may have been worshipped there as a form of the Arabian sun-god Shams.

Bahrain is a kingdom, a semi-constitutional monarchy since 2002, with a bicameral National Assembly. Its capital and largest city is Manama. The King Fahd Causeway, completed in December 1986, links it with the Saudi Arabian mainland. It has been ruled by the Al Khalifa family since 1783 and became independent from the United Kingdom in 1971.
banabhatta: What is known of Bana's ancestry and early life is reconstructed from his own words: the introductory verses attached to the Kadambari and the first two chapters, or ucchvasas, of the Harshacharita. He was born to Chitrabhanu and Rajadevi in the village of Pritikuta, in a Kanyakubja Brahmin family. His mother died early and left him in the care of his father, who married again and had two more sons.

His father died when Bana was fourteen. For a time he led a colourful, wandering life with his half-brothers, and afterwards he came back to his native village. There, on a summer day, he received a letter from Krishna, a cousin of Harsha, and went to meet the king, who was camping near the town of Manitara. Harsha received him at first with mock signs of anger and then showed him much favour. Bana became the court poet during Harsha's reign at Kanyakubja.

The Harshacharita, whose title means the deeds of Harsha, was Bana's first composition; its third chapter describes the circumstances in which he came to write it. It is considered the first Indian work that may be regarded as a historical biography and the beginning of historical poetic writing in Sanskrit, and it gives a vivid picture of life in the Indian countryside.

Bana died before he could finish the Kadambari, and his son Bhushanabhatta completed it. Two further works are attributed to him, the Chandikashataka and a drama, the Parvatiparinaya. A Sanskrit saying, Banochhistam jagatsarvam, holds that Bana described everything in the world and left nothing out. The Harshacharita was translated into English by E. B. Cowell and F. W. Thomas for the Royal Asiatic Society in 1897.
bangkok: Bangkok lies in the Chao Phraya River delta in Thailand's central plain. The river flows southwards through the city and empties into the Gulf of Thailand about 25 kilometres south of the centre. The area is flat and low-lying, with an average elevation of 1.5 metres above sea level. Most of it was originally swampland, gradually drained and irrigated by canals (khlong) dug between the 16th and 19th centuries. The origin of the name is unclear. Bang is a Thai word for a village on a stream, and the name may derive from Bang Ko, 'island', or from Bang Makok, after a plant bearing olive-like fruit.

The history of Bangkok goes back at least to the early 15th century, when it was a village on the west bank of the Chao Phraya under Ayutthaya. It served as a customs outpost with forts on both sides of the river, and was the site of a siege in 1688 in which the French were expelled from Siam. After Ayutthaya fell to the Burmese in 1767, King Taksin made the town his capital. The City Pillar was erected on 21 April 1782, regarded as the date of the city's foundation as the capital, and foreign visitors continued to call it Bangkok.

The city was at the heart of the modernisation of Siam in the late 19th century. Charoen Krung Road, the first built by Western techniques, was completed in 1864, and rail transport was introduced in 1893. Through the 20th century the city was at the centre of political struggles, as Siam abolished absolute monarchy and adopted constitutional rule. It became a special administrative area under the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration in 1972.

Bangkok is governed by the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration and is a special administrative area at provincial level, divided into fifty districts. Its landmarks include the Grand Palace and the Buddhist temples Wat Arun and Wat Pho. Thailand's five oldest universities, Chulalongkorn, Thammasat, Kasetsart, Mahidol and Silpakorn, founded between 1917 and 1943, are in the city.
barcelona: Barcelona lies on the north-east coast of the Iberian Peninsula, facing the Mediterranean Sea, on a plain about 5 km wide limited by the Collserola mountain range, the Llobregat river to the south-west and the Besòs river to the north. It lies 120 km south of the Pyrenees. The escarpment of Montjuïc overlooks the harbour and is topped by Montjuïc Castle, a fortress built in the 17th and 18th centuries to control the city.

According to tradition Barcelona was founded by Phoenician or Carthaginian settlers, and some historians credit the Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca with naming it Barcino in the 3rd century BCE, though this theory has been questioned. Coins of the 3rd century BCE found at the foot of Montjuïc carry the name Barkeno in Iberian script.

In the Middle Ages Barcelona became the capital of the County of Barcelona. After the union with Aragon it remained capital of the Principality of Catalonia and the most important city of the Crown of Aragon, until Valencia overtook it shortly before 1516. Its industrial rise began in 1833, when Catalonia's textile industry began to use steam power. It became capital of autonomous Catalonia in 1931 and was taken by the fascists in 1939.

Barcelona is the capital of Catalonia and the second most populous municipality of Spain. Its old centre, the Barri Gòtic, has buildings from medieval times and some from the Roman settlement. Works of Antoni Gaudí and Lluís Domènech i Montaner are World Heritage Sites, and the city hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics.
battle-of-albulena: Skanderbeg had fought the Ottoman Empire since 1444, and after more than a decade of war his resources were worn out. His siege of Berat in 1455 ended in catastrophe when an Ottoman counterattack fell on the Albanians during his temporary absence. Afterwards some of his most trusted officers deserted. Moisi Golemi returned in May 1456 at the head of an Ottoman force, was defeated at the Battle of Oranik and was taken back without punishment.

A graver loss was his nephew Hamza Kastrioti, one of his most important officers, who had grown dissatisfied with Skanderbeg's increasing power and was promised control of much of Albania once it was conquered. Relations with Venice were at their lowest point. Alfonso V of Aragon and Pope Calixtus III, his allies, could not provide for him fully, and a fleet the pope promised in 1457 did not arrive.

By the end of May 1457 an Ottoman army of between 50,000 and 80,000 men approached, against which Skanderbeg had between 8,000 and 10,000. He stalled the akıncı vanguard marching through Dibër, then withdrew before the main force. Since both Ottoman commanders knew his usual ambushes, he split his army into several groups and ordered them to march through the forests and mountains in different directions, supplied by the local people and by depots, and not to assemble or attack without his word.

The Ottomans pillaged the Mat valley and camped at Albulena, north of Mount Tumenishta and south of modern Laç. Through July and August Skanderbeg stayed out of sight, and rumours spread that he had fled. On 2 September his reassembled army attacked the camp in three groups with a great noise of clashing metal. The Ottomans, believing the attackers more numerous than they were, panicked. Their dead may have been as many as 30,000, though it is unlikely that more than 15,000 were killed; 15,000 were taken prisoner and twenty-four standards were captured.

Hamza Kastrioti was captured and sent as a prisoner to Naples. An Ottoman envoy came to ransom the standard bearers and forty distinguished prisoners and proposed a truce, which Skanderbeg would accept only if Svetigrad and Berat were restored to him. In 1460 Sultan Mehmed II and Skanderbeg signed an armistice that lasted three years, giving Skanderbeg the opportunity to cross to Italy and help Ferdinand I of Naples. The historian Franz Babinger called the battle Skanderbeg's most brilliant victory. Desertions from his army became rare afterwards, but the war continued until the fall of Krujë in 1478.
battle-of-bir-hakeim: Bir Hakeim was a fortress built by the Ottomans at the crossing of two Bedouin paths. It stood at the southern end of the Gazala line, a series of brigade-sized defensive boxes that the British Eighth Army held west of Tobruk. On 14 February 1942 the 1st Free French Brigade took over the box, which was surrounded by 50,000 mines. The brigade had a fighting strength of 3,000 men, with the 13th Demi-Brigade of the Foreign Legion as its backbone, and by mid-May it had dug 1,200 entrenchments, foxholes and gun emplacements. The Axis plan sent the armour around the box while the Italian 132nd Armoured Division Ariete neutralised it.

On the morning of 27 May an Italian tank battalion of the Ariete Division, with 60 tanks, charged the minefield and wire. It lost 31 tanks and a self-propelled gun, and ten tanks that got through were knocked out by 75 mm anti-tank guns. From 2 June the position was shelled and bombed, and Stuka dive-bombers raided it more than twenty times, but the well-built positions were almost invulnerable. On 6 June the 90th Light Division attacked with pioneers, who cleared passages through the minefields.

From 8 June Rommel directed attacks from the north with part of the 15th Panzer Division, and the perimeter was forced back. On 10 June, with ammunition almost gone, the fort took the largest air raid of the siege, by 100 Stukas. After dark sappers cleared a narrow passage through the mines on the western face. Kœnig left at the head of the column in a car driven by Susan Travers, an Englishwoman serving with the Foreign Legion, and most of the brigade broke through troops of the 90th Light Division to reach lorries and ambulances sent by the British 7th Motor Brigade.

Thomas Buell and Ken Ford give the French losses as 141 dead, 229 wounded and 814 taken prisoner, with 53 guns and 50 vehicles; the Axis lost 3,300 dead or wounded and 227 captured, with 164 vehicles destroyed and 49 aircraft shot down. The defence had lengthened the Axis supply route around the Gazala line and gave the British time to recover from their defeat in the Cauldron, and the delay influenced the cancellation of Operation Herkules, the Axis invasion of Malta. Tobruk still fell ten days later. Both sides used the battle for propaganda, and Winston Churchill declared the Free French to be the Fighting French.
battle-of-koppam: From his accession Rajadhiraja Chola I sought to subdue the Chalukyas, who ruled parts of northern Karnataka and the south of present-day Maharashtra, and to add their lands to the Chola Empire. His first invasion, in 1047–48, had failed. On the second expedition he led a large army north and plundered the province of Rattamandalam, with his brother and heir-apparent Rajendra Chola II following in the rear.

According to the Chola sources and the Thiruvalandur copper plate, Rajadhiraja had personally led the attack on Kalyanapura, also called Kalyani, the modern Basavakalyan. Someshvara I fled when the city was attacked, returned with an army and was beaten again, and the Chola king then withdrew towards Kollapura. The copper plate says that Someshvara gathered a huge army and called out for battle as the Chola withdrew, and that the Chola turned to meet him at the place called Koppam.

The copper plate describes columns of foot soldiers, horses and elephants engaging their counterparts, with Rajadhiraja fighting from his elephant until a downpour of Chalukya arrows killed him. The Chola troops, who had been holding the upper hand, panicked and began to retreat. Rajendra II, commanding the reserve, took over the army, rallied it and inflicted heavy losses, forcing Someshvara to flee. Chola sources record that the elephants, horses and camels of the Chalukyas, a large booty and the queens of Someshvara fell into Chola hands. Rajendra is reported to have set up a victory pillar at Kolhapur before returning to his country.

The battle is known chiefly from the Chola side: an inscription dated to 1054 and Rajendra Chola II's Manimangalam record of 1055. The latter gives the victory to Rajendra and says that Ahavamalla, as it calls the Chalukya king, became afraid, incurred disgrace and ran away. The year is given as 1054, or as 1052 by the historian Sen. The site is also uncertain. The Manimangalam inscription places Koppam on the bank of the great river; the scholar Fleet identified it with Khidrapur, 30 miles south-east of Kolhapur, taking the river to be the Krishna, while other historians have put it near Maski.
beijing: Beijing is situated at the northern edge of the roughly triangular North China Plain, which opens to the south and east of the city. Mountains to the north, northwest and west shield the city and northern China's agricultural heartland from the encroaching desert steppes. The Great Wall of China across the northern part of the municipality was built on the rugged topography to defend against nomadic incursions from the steppes. The highest point of the municipality is Mount Dongling, at 2,303 metres, in the Western Hills on the border with Hebei.

The name Beijing means 'Northern Capital' and was applied to the city in 1403, during the Ming dynasty, to distinguish it from Nanjing, the 'Southern Capital'. The older English spelling Peking was used by the Jesuit missionary Martino Martini in an atlas published in Amsterdam in 1655. Over the past 3,000 years the city has had numerous other names.

The earliest traces of human habitation in the municipality were found in the caves of Dragon Bone Hill near the village of Zhoukoudian, where Peking Man lived. Homo erectus fossils from the caves date to 230,000 to 250,000 years ago, and Homo sapiens lived there more recently, about 27,000 years ago. Neolithic settlements have been found throughout the municipality, including in Wangfujing in central Beijing.

The first walled city in the area was Ji, the capital of the state of Ji, located around the present Guang'anmen area in the south of Xicheng District. During the early Zhou period the settlement was conquered by the state of Yan, which made it its new capital. Its original capital lay 45 kilometres to the southwest in Fangshan District. Yan eventually became one of the seven major states of China in the Warring States period.

Beijing is the capital of China and is governed as a provincial-level municipality with 16 districts. In 2024 its population was about 21.8 million. Its traditional housing consists of siheyuans, courtyard houses, and the narrow alleys between them called hutongs. It has eight UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Summer Palace, the Ming Tombs, the Zhoukoudian Peking Man Site and parts of the Great Wall and the Grand Canal. Beijing opera is its best-known traditional form of theatre.
belarus: Belarus is a landlocked country of 207,600 square kilometres, lying between latitudes 51° and 57° N and measuring 560 kilometres from north to south and 650 from west to east. It is relatively flat, with large tracts of marshy land, about 40% forest, and 11,000 lakes.

Three major rivers run through it: the Neman flows west toward the Baltic Sea, the Pripyat flows east to the Dnieper, and the Dnieper flows south toward the Black Sea. The highest point is Dzyarzhynskaya Hara, at 345 metres. About 70% of the radiation from the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster in neighbouring Ukraine entered Belarusian territory, and about a fifth of the land was affected by fallout.

Baltic tribes first permanently settled the region in the 3rd century, and around the 5th century the Slavs took it over, and the gradual assimilation of the Baltic settlers into Slavic culture was peaceful. In the 9th century it became part of Kievan Rus', a vast East Slavic state ruled by the Rurikids, which split into independent principalities on the death of Yaroslav the Wise in 1054.

The Battle on the Nemiga River in 1067 is considered the founding date of Minsk. The lands avoided the brunt of the 13th-century Mongol invasion and joined the Grand Duchy of Lithuania; the annals affirm an alliance and united foreign policy between Polotsk and Lithuania for decades. The duchy fought alongside Poland against the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Grunwald in 1410.

By the 14th century the lands had come fully under the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and later the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, a period lasting 500 years until the partitions of 1792–1795 placed Belarus within the Russian Empire for the first time. The Byelorussian SSR, formed after the Russian Revolution, became a founding republic of the Soviet Union in 1922. After the Polish-Soviet War (1918–1921) Belarus lost almost half its territory to Poland, and in the Second World War it lost about a quarter of its population and half of its economic resources. Many prominent Belarusian intellectuals were exiled or killed in Stalinist purges in the 1930s.

Belarus proclaimed its sovereignty on 27 July 1990 and gained independence on 25 August 1991. Belarus and Russia signed a treaty in 2000 forming the Union State. The official languages are Russian and Belarusian. Francysk Skaryna's Bible, published between 1517 and 1525, was the first book printed in Belarus or anywhere in Eastern Europe.
belgium: Belgium covers 30,689 square kilometres in the Low Countries, bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, France and the North Sea. It has three main geographical regions: the coastal plain in the northwest, with sand dunes and polders; the central plateau, a slowly rising landscape of fertile valleys and the sandy plain of the Campine; and the forested, rugged Ardennes in the southeast. The highest point is the Signal de Botrange, at 694 metres. The climate is maritime temperate, with significant precipitation in all seasons.

In his account of the conquest of Gaul, Julius Caesar described the Belgae as inhabiting northern Gaul between the Seine and Marne rivers and the Rhine, and as the bravest of the Gauls. The northernmost tribes, including the Menapii, Nervii and Atuatuci, held most of modern Belgium. After Caesar's conquests the Roman province of Gallia Belgica covered most of northern Gaul, and the eastern part of modern Belgium lay in Germania Inferior. As Roman central government collapsed, the provinces were inhabited by Romanised populations and Germanic-speaking Franks, who came to dominate military and political life.

The region was later part of the Carolingian Empire, the Holy Roman Empire and the Burgundian Netherlands, and was ruled by Habsburg Spain (1556–1714), the Austrian Habsburgs (1714–1794) and Revolutionary France (1794–1815). Most of it joined the United Kingdom of the Netherlands after the Congress of Vienna in 1815. Being contested by so many powers gave Belgium the name the Battlefield of Europe.

An independent Belgium was established in 1830 after the Belgian Revolution. It was the first country in continental Europe to industrialise, and mining and steelmaking in Liège Province and around Charleroi made it one of the three most industrialised nations in the world from 1830 to 1910, although Flanders suffered famine from 1846 to 1850.

Belgium is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy and a federal state of three regions, Flanders, Wallonia and the Brussels-Capital Region, with Dutch-speaking, French-speaking and small German-speaking communities. Tensions between Dutch-speakers and French-speakers rose in the second half of the twentieth century and led to reforms that turned a unitary state into a federal one between 1970 and 1993. After the 2010 federal election the country went a record 589 days without forming a government. Brussels hosts the seats of several European Union institutions, and the country's colonies, the Belgian Congo and Ruanda-Urundi, became independent between 1960 and 1962.
berlin: Berlin lies in low-lying marshy woodland on the Northern European Plain, along the Spree, which empties into the Havel in the western borough of Spandau. The Spree follows the Berliner Urstromtal, an ice-age glacial valley between the Barnim Plateau to the north and the Teltow plateau to the south, formed by meltwater at the end of the last glaciation. About a third of the city's area is forests, parks, gardens, rivers, canals and lakes. The name has roots in the language of the West Slavs and may be related to the Old Polabian stem berl-/birl-, 'swamp'. Five of the twelve boroughs bear Slavic-derived names, among them Pankow and Spandau.

The area has been settled for millennia: a deer mask of about 9,000 BCE is attributed to the Maglemosian culture, and dense settlement along the Spree and Havel gave rise to the Lusatian culture around 2,000 BCE. Germanic tribes settled from about 500 BCE, the Burgundians followed the Semnones after about 200 CE, and in the 7th century Slavic tribes, later known as the Hevelli and Sprevane, reached the region.

Berlin was first documented in the 13th century, at the crossing of two important trade routes. It was capital of the Margraviate of Brandenburg from 1417, the Kingdom of Prussia from 1701 and the German Empire from 1871. In 1685 the Edict of Potsdam granted religious freedom and tax-free status to French Huguenot refugees.

The Greater Berlin Act of 1920 raised the population from 1.9 million to 4 million, and in the 1920s Berlin was the third-largest city in the world. It was capital of the Weimar Republic and of Nazi Germany until 1945. After the Second World War it was split into West Berlin and East Berlin, divided by the Berlin Wall, and Bonn became the West German capital. Berlin again became the capital of all Germany after reunification on 3 October 1990.

Berlin covers 891 km2 and is the most populous city proper in the European Union. Since 1990 it has been one of three city-states among the 16 states of Germany, governed by the Senate and the 141-seat Abgeordnetenhaus. The bombing of the Second World War devastated the city, and many surviving buildings were later demolished; after reunification many heritage structures were reconstructed.

Museum Island, designated a district dedicated to art and antiquities by royal decree in 1841, is one of three UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Charité hospital traces its origins to 1710, and Robert Koch and Rudolf Virchow worked in Berlin. The city hosted the 1936 Summer Olympics.
bodleian-library: The first purpose-built library known at Oxford was founded in the 14th century under the will of Thomas Cobham, Bishop of Worcester (d. 1327): a small collection of chained books kept above the north side of the University Church of St Mary the Virgin. When Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, gave a great collection of manuscripts between 1435 and 1437 a larger room was needed, and one was built above the Divinity School and completed in 1488; it is still known as Duke Humfrey's Library.

In the later 16th century the library declined. Its furniture was sold, and only three of Duke Humphrey's original books remained. In 1598 Thomas Bodley, a former fellow of Merton College, wrote to the Vice Chancellor offering to restore it at his own cost. The room was refitted, Bodley gave some of his own books, and the library was formally reopened on 8 November 1602 with around 2,000 books.

In 1610 Bodley made an agreement with the Stationers' Company, suggested by the first librarian, Thomas James, that a copy of every book registered with the company would be placed in the library. The collection grew so fast that the building was extended between 1610 and 1612, and the Schools Quadrangle was built between 1613 and 1619. By 1620 there were 16,000 items. John Selden left his books and manuscripts to the library in 1654. Until the establishment of the British Museum in 1753 the Bodleian was effectively the national library of England.

The library took over the neighbouring Radcliffe Camera in 1860, and the Copyright Act of 1911 continued the Stationers' agreement by making it a library of legal deposit. Its holdings passed one million books in 1914. The New Bodleian, designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott, was completed in 1940; rebuilt behind its original façade, it reopened as the Weston Library on 21 March 2015.

The Bodleian works principally as a reference library, and documents may not be taken from the reading rooms. New readers must agree to a formal declaration not to remove, mark or damage anything in the library, nor to bring fire or flame into it. Its head is known as Bodley's Librarian; 25 people have held the office. Since 2000 it has been the largest member of a group of Oxford libraries, called the Bodleian Libraries since 2010. With over 13 million printed items it is the second-largest library in Britain after the British Library, and its principal store is at South Marston.
bolivia: Bolivia is a landlocked country of 1,098,581 square kilometres in central South America, the fifth largest in the continent. Its geography consists of an Andean region in the west and tropical lowlands in the east and north, and it includes the Altiplano plateau, temperate valleys, the Gran Chaco and part of the Amazon plain. Elevations range from 6,542 metres at Nevado Sajama to nearly 70 metres along the Paraguay River.

In the Andean southwest lie Lake Titicaca, the highest commercially navigable lake in the world and the largest lake in South America, and the Salar de Uyuni, the largest salt flat in the world and an important source of lithium.

Tiwanaku, with its capital at Tiwanaku in western Bolivia, dates back as early as 1500 BCE, when it was a small agricultural village. It grew to urban proportions between 600 and 800 CE and, around 400 CE, began expanding its reach into the Yungas by creating colonies, fostering trade agreements and instituting state cults. As rainfall gradually decreased, food stores shrank and the elites lost power, and Tiwanaku disappeared around 1000 CE. Between 1438 and 1527 the Inca Empire expanded from Cusco into the region.

The Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire began in 1524 and was mostly completed by 1533. The territory was known as Charcas, with local government from the Audiencia de Charcas at La Plata, modern Sucre. Potosí, founded in 1545 as a mining town, became the largest city in the New World, with a population exceeding 150,000. After an unsuccessful rebellion in Sucre on 25 May 1809, sixteen years of fighting preceded the establishment of the republic. Antonio José de Sucre chose to create a new state rather than join Peru or the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, and on 6 August 1825 named it in honour of Simón Bolívar.

The name Bolivia was approved on 3 October 1825. In the 19th and early 20th centuries the country lost peripheral territories, among them the Pacific coastal region seized by Chile in 1879. The Bolivian National Revolution of 1952 established universal suffrage and nationalised the tin mines.

La Paz is the seat of government and Sucre the constitutional capital, while Santa Cruz de la Sierra is the largest city. Bolivia is a constitutionally unitary state divided into nine departments, and since 2009 its official name has been the Plurinational State of Bolivia. Spanish is the official and predominant language, and 36 indigenous languages also have official status, of which Guaraní, Aymara and Quechua are most commonly spoken. Major archaeological ruins include Tiwanaku, El Fuerte de Samaipata, Inkallaqta and Iskanwaya.
botswana: Botswana has a total area of 581,730 square kilometres and is topographically flat, with approximately 70% of its territory part of the Kalahari Desert. It borders South Africa, Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe. The terrain consists of sandy soils, rocky hill ranges and grasslands, and the climate is generally semi-arid, with highly seasonal rainfall. The north and east receive more rain than the dry southwest, and much of the population lives in the southeast.

In the northwest the Okavango River spreads across the Kalahari in a vast inland delta of channels, lagoons, islands and seasonal wetlands, rather than flowing to the sea. The Chobe River in the north forms part of the border with Namibia.

Stone tools in present-day Botswana date back two million years, and the ancestors of the Khoe and the San lived in the region 30,000 to 40,000 years ago. Rock art dates back approximately 30,000 years. Around 2,000 years ago people introduced cattle, sheep, pottery and agriculture. Bantu-speaking peoples migrated into the region between 2,000 and 1,500 years ago: the Kalanga arrived around 200 CE and the ancestors of the Tswana around 400 CE, bringing iron and copper tools and establishing permanent settlements. Trade expanded from the seventh century, and the Toutswe people, the Kingdom of Mapungubwe and later Great Zimbabwe became important regional powers, with cattle and gold playing major economic roles.

From the fifteenth to the eighteenth century Tswana and Kalanga peoples formed new political communities. Tswana society was organised into merafe, governed by chiefs called dikgosi. The Difaqane of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth century caused widespread warfare and migration, and by the 1840s many states had been re-established and were governed through the kgotla, a traditional community council. Missionaries arrived in 1816, followed by British traders and explorers, and David Livingstone established a mission in 1845. The discovery of the Tati Goldfields in 1868 led to a gold rush and the growth of Francistown. In 1885 the British declared the protectorate of Bechuanaland, which became independent on 30 September 1966.

Gaborone is the capital and largest city. Botswana is a parliamentary republic, and its government draws on both the Westminster system and the tribal governments of the Tswana. English is the official language and Setswana is widely spoken. The Tswana make up about 79% of the population, the Kalanga about 11% and the San about 3%. Botswana is a member of the Southern African Development Community, the Commonwealth of Nations and the United Nations.
brazil: Brazil covers 8,515,767 square kilometres, nearly half of the land area of South America (47.7%), and borders every South American country except Ecuador and Chile. Its Atlantic coastline is 7,491 kilometres long. The country contains most of the Amazon basin, with the world's largest river system and most extensive tropical forest, together with wetlands, savannas, plateaus and low mountains. It is the only country that both the equator and the Tropic of Capricorn cross, and it spans four time zones. Most of its territory is tropical, with equatorial rainforest in the north, semiarid land in the northeast and temperate forest in the south.

Human remains found at Pedro Leopoldo, in Minas Gerais, show habitation going back at least 11,000 years, and the earliest pottery found in the Western Hemisphere, near Santarém, was dated to over 8,000 years ago. The Marajoara culture flourished on Marajó from 400 to 1400 CE. When the Portuguese arrived, the territory had an estimated Indigenous population of 7 million people, mostly semi-nomadic, among them the Tupis, Guaranis and Gês.

The land was claimed for Portugal on 22 April 1500 by the fleet of Pedro Álvares Cabral, after the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494. São Vicente was founded in 1532, and in 1534 King John III of Portugal divided the territory into fifteen private captaincies. The system failed, and in 1549 the king created the Governorate General of Brazil at Salvador. In the first two centuries Indigenous and European groups lived in constant war, forming opportunistic alliances.

Brazil became a united kingdom with Portugal in 1815, after the Portuguese court moved to Rio de Janeiro. Prince Pedro of Braganza declared independence in 1822 and founded the Empire of Brazil after a war with Portugal. The constitution of 1824 set up a bicameral legislature, and slavery was gradually abolished until its final abolition in 1888. A military coup in 1889 made the country a presidential republic. A revolution in 1930 brought Getúlio Vargas to power, and his self-coup of 1937 began the authoritarian Estado Novo. Democracy returned after 1945, a military dictatorship ruled from 1964 to 1985, and the present constitution dates from 1988.

Brazil is a federation of 26 states and a Federal District, which holds the capital, Brasília; São Paulo is the most populous city. The 2022 census counted 203 million people, and 45.3% described themselves as Pardo, 43.5% as White, 10.2% as Black and 0.6% as Indigenous. Its culture derives mainly from Portuguese culture, shaped also by African, Indigenous and other European traditions and by Italians, Germans, Japanese, Jewish and Arab immigrants in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
brihatkatha: The date of the work is uncertain. Gunadhya may have flourished under a Satavahana king of Pratishthana, the modern Paithan in Maharashtra; according to D. C. Sircar he probably lived between the 1st century BCE and the 3rd century CE. Another account, in the Nepala Mahatmya of the Skanda Purana, makes him a native of Mathura and court poet of King Madana of Ujjain, a tradition Sircar calls less authentic. Paishachi, the language he used, is a little-known Prakrit, described as the speech of the common people of the border regions of northwest India.

The earliest surviving reference seems to be that of Subandhu in his Vasavadatta, and Banabhatta refers to the work in the Harshacharita and the Kadambari. Dandin, in the Kavyadarsha, calls it marvellous and says it was composed in the vernacular of the bhutas, though his information appears to be second-hand. A Cambodian inscription of about 875 names Gunadhya, and the Kannada Kavirajamarga of about 850 mentions a Sanskrit version, now lost, by Durvinita. A romantic work by Gunadhya can safely be assumed to have existed before 600 CE.

The adaptations differ too much for the original to be reconstructed whole, but what they share allows strong inferences. The life of Udayana of Kaushambi served as a prelude: his upbringing in a hermitage after a monstrous bird carried off his pregnant mother, his captivity under Pradyota, king of Ujjayini, his elopement with Pradyota's daughter Vasavadatta, and his second marriage to Padmavati, arranged by ministers who made him believe Vasavadatta dead. The central story was that of their son Naravahanadatta, born as a boon of Kubera and fated to become emperor of the Vidyadharas. Kshemendra's version is in eighteen books called lambakas, as the original is thought to have been.

Besides the two Kashmiri versions, the story is known from the Sanskrit Brihatkathashlokasamgraha of Budhasvamin, of which the complete text has not been found, and from the Perunkatai and the Vasudevahimdi in vernacular languages. Dandin states that the original was in prose, not in the verse of the Kashmiri recensions. Scholars compare Gunadhya with Vyasa and Valmiki, and the disappearance of his text is counted a very great loss to Indian literature.
budapest: Budapest stands on the River Danube, at the centre of the Pannonian Basin, on an ancient route linking the hills of Transdanubia with the Great Plain. The names Buda and Pest are of obscure origin. Buda was probably the name of the first constable of the fortress built on Castle Hill in the 11th century, or derives from a personal name of Turkic origin, Bod or Bud, meaning 'twig'. Before the unification of 1873 the towns together were sometimes called Pest-Buda. In colloquial Hungarian, Buda means the districts west of the Danube, including the former Óbuda, and Pest those to the east. The city is now divided into 23 districts.

The first settlement on the territory of Budapest was built by Celts before 1 CE and was later occupied by the Romans. The Roman settlement of Aquincum became the main city of Pannonia Inferior in 106 CE. It began as a military settlement, around which a city gradually rose, and its site corresponds to the Óbuda district. The Romans built roads, amphitheatres, baths and houses with heated floors. The area east of the Danube was outside the Roman Empire and remained Germanic and Sarmatian in character.

After the foundation of Hungary in the late 9th century the area was pillaged by the Mongols in 1241. It became the royal seat in 1361, and under Matthias Corvinus Buda was by the 15th century one of the European centres of Renaissance culture. The siege of Buda in 1541 was followed by nearly 150 years of Ottoman rule, and after the reconquest of Buda in 1686 the region entered an age of prosperity. The city was the focal point of the Hungarian Revolution of 1848, the Battle of Budapest in 1945 and the Hungarian Revolution of 1956. In 1896 it opened the first underground transit line on the European continent, now the M1 Millennium Underground.

Budapest is the seat of the Hungarian national government, and the National Assembly sits in the neo-Gothic Hungarian Parliament, the largest building in the country. The historic centre along the Danube, with Buda Castle and the 13th-century Matthias Church, is a World Heritage Site, as are the Castle Hill, the Danube embankments and Andrássy út. Other landmarks include the State Opera House, St Stephen's Basilica, which displays the Holy Right Hand of Hungary's first king, and the Roman remains of the Aquincum Museum. The city has been a spa destination since Roman times, with more than 100 medicinal geothermal springs.
buddhism: Buddhism is based on teachings attributed to the Buddha, a wandering ascetic and religious teacher who lived in South Asia in the 6th or 5th century BCE, the 5th century being the best estimate. The accounts of his life in the early texts are inconsistent. They give his family name as Gautama and place his birth at Lumbini, in present-day Nepal. Legends make his father a king named Suddhodana, but scholars such as Richard Gombrich doubt this, since the evidence suggests he came from the Shakya community, governed by a small oligarchy or council.

The roots of the religion lie in the intellectual ferment of Iron Age India around the middle of the first millennium BCE, the period of the Upanishads and the rise of the Śramaṇa movements, which included Buddhism and Jainism.

According to tradition, the Buddha taught a path that leads to release from dukkha, suffering or unsatisfactoriness, by reaching nirvana, the extinguishing of the passions. He regarded it as a Middle Way between extreme asceticism and sensory indulgence. The Four Noble Truths hold that everything is impermanent, yet people crave and cling to impermanent things, which is dukkha, and that the Noble Eightfold Path leads out of the cycle of rebirth. Taking the Three Refuges, in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, is the traditional first step in most schools.

The Buddha's words were first passed on orally, and the first canonical texts were probably written down in Sri Lanka about 400 years after his death. Scholars generally recognise two surviving branches, Theravāda and Mahāyāna. Theravada holds the Pali Canon as its only authority, and Mahayana, with roots in the 1st century BCE, also honours later literature and stresses the Bodhisattva ideal of working for the liberation of all beings. Vajrayāna, which includes esoteric tantric techniques, may be seen as a separate branch or part of Mahayana.

Buddhism spread gradually through much of Asia along the Silk Road and reached the West in the 19th century. Until the early second millennium it was widely practised in the Indian subcontinent before declining there. Learning centres such as Nalanda and Vikramashila preserved classical Indian disciplines, including grammar, astronomy and medicine, and taught foreign students from across Asia. The religion influenced the cultures of Asia deeply, in philosophy, art, architecture and festivals, and shaped the development of Hinduism, Taoism and Confucianism.
buenos-aires: Buenos Aires lies on the southwest shore of the Río de la Plata, which is called the world's widest river, in the pampa region. Several districts, among them Puerto Madero and the main port, were built on land reclaimed along the river. The area was once crossed by streams and lagoons. As floods damaged the city's infrastructure in 1908, many streams were channelled, and from 1919 most were enclosed. The Maldonado was tubed in 1954 and now runs below Juan B. Justo Avenue. The city is laid out on a rectangular grid of square blocks, 110 metres long, called manzanas.

The name comes from Santa Maria de los Buenos Aires, Holy Mary of the Good Winds. Spanish sailors, especially Andalusians, invoked the Virgin of the Buen Ayre, named after Our Lady of Bonaria in Cagliari, Sardinia. Juan Díaz de Solís was the first European to reach the Río de la Plata, in 1516, and was killed in an attack by the Charrúa. Pedro de Mendoza founded the city on 2 February 1536, in what is now the San Telmo district.

Attacks by indigenous people forced the settlers away, and the site was abandoned in 1541 or 1542. A second and permanent settlement was established on 11 June 1580 by Juan de Garay, who came down the Paraná River from Asunción. He named it Santísima Trinidad, and its port became the Puerto de Santa María de los Buenos Aires. Later rule is grouped as Habsburg Spain to 1700, Bourbon Spain to 1808, the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata from 1810 and the Argentine Confederation from 1831. The State of Buenos Aires existed from 1852 to 1861.

In 1880, after the Argentine Civil War, the city was federalised and split from Buenos Aires Province, and its limits grew to include Belgrano and Flores. Since the 19th century the city and country have received millions of immigrants from many parts of the world. The Parque Tres de Febrero was inaugurated on 11 November 1875, and the Botanical Gardens on 7 September 1898, both later work of the French Argentine urbanist Carlos Thays.

Buenos Aires is the capital and largest city of Argentina. A constitutional amendment of 1994 gave it autonomy, hence its formal name, the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires, and its citizens elected their first chief of government in 1996. The city proper had 2,891,082 residents at the 2010 census, with 13,147,638 in Greater Buenos Aires. It is home to the Teatro Colón, an opera house, and to the Avenida 9 de Julio, 140 metres wide. The city joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network in 2005 as a City of Design.
bulgaria: Bulgaria covers 110,994 square kilometres in the east of the Balkans, south of the Danube and west of the Black Sea, with a coastline of 354 kilometres. Its main topographical features are the Danubian Plain, the Balkan Mountains, the Upper Thracian Plain and the Rila-Rhodope massif. The Balkan Mountains run from west to east through the middle of the country, and Musala, at 2,925 metres, is the highest point in both Bulgaria and the Balkans. Plains occupy about a third of the territory and plateaux and hills 41%. The climate is varied and changeable because the country lies at the meeting point of Mediterranean, Oceanic and Continental air masses.

Neanderthal remains of around 150,000 years ago are among the earliest traces of human activity, and the Karanovo culture arose c. 6,500 BCE. The Varna culture is credited with the invention of goldworking and produced the oldest golden jewellery in the world, over 6,000 years old. The Thracians appeared on the Balkan Peninsula before the 12th century BCE, and after the defeat of the second Persian invasion in 479 BCE most of the tribes united under king Teres to form the Odrysian kingdom.
Philip II of Macedon vassalised it in 341 BCE, and it became a Roman province in 45 CE. In the 6th century the Slavs entered the Balkans and assimilated the Thracians.

The Bulgars, led by Asparuh, permanently invaded the Balkans in the late 7th century and established the First Bulgarian Empire, recognised by the Byzantine Empire in 681. It dominated most of the Balkans and influenced Slavic cultures through the Cyrillic script, which the Preslav Literary School developed. It lasted until the early 11th century, when the Byzantine emperor Basil II conquered and dismantled it.

A revolt in 1185 established the Second Bulgarian Empire, which reached its apex under Ivan Asen II (1218–1241), and in 1396 the empire, weakened by wars and feudal strife, fell under Ottoman rule for nearly five centuries.

The Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78 resulted in the third and current Bulgarian state, which declared independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1908. Many ethnic Bulgarians were left outside its borders, which stoked irredentist sentiment, conflicts with neighbours and alliances with Germany in both world wars.

In 1946 Bulgaria came under the Soviet-led Eastern Bloc as a socialist state, and the Communist Party gave up its monopoly on power after the revolutions of 1989. It has been a parliamentary republic of 28 provinces since the constitution of 1991, and a member of the European Union and NATO.
burkina-faso: Burkina Faso covers 274,223 square kilometres. Most of the country is a peneplain, a gently undulating landscape with a few isolated hills that are the last vestiges of a Precambrian massif. The southwest is a sandstone massif, bordered by cliffs up to 150 metres high, where the highest peak, Ténakourou, rises to 749 metres. The country owed its former name, Upper Volta, to three rivers, the Black Volta (Mouhoun), the White Volta (Nakambé) and the Red Volta (Nazinon). Only the Black Volta and the Komoé flow year-round, and water shortages are often a problem in the north.

The northwest was populated by hunter-gatherers from about 14,000 BCE to 5,000 BCE, and agricultural settlements were established between 3600 and 2600 BCE. The oldest evidence of iron smelting in Burkina Faso dates from 800 to 700 BCE and forms part of the Ancient Ferrous Metallurgy World Heritage Site. The Bura culture existed in the southeast from the 3rd to the 13th century CE.

From medieval times until the end of the 19th century the central region was ruled by the Mossi, descendants of Dagomba warriors from present-day Ghana who mixed with Mandé and other local peoples in the 11th century. They established separate kingdoms, among them Tenkodogo, Yatenga, Zandoma and Ouagadougou, and defended their territory, beliefs and social structure against attempts at conquest and conversion from Muslims to the northwest.

The Tarikh al-Sudan reports that a Mossi ruler took control of Timbuktu between 1328 and 1338, during the reign of Mansa Musa, and the Tarikh al-fattash describes conflicts between the 15th-century Mossi king Komdao and the Songhay ruler Sonni Ali. The Mossi were defeated at the Battle of Kobi in 1483. The French colonised the area in 1896 as part of French West Africa, and it became fully independent in 1960 as the Republic of Upper Volta. On 4 August 1984 President Thomas Sankara renamed it Burkina Faso.

Ouagadougou is the capital and largest city. The name joins Burkina, from Mooré, meaning upright, with Faso, from Dyula, meaning fatherland. The country is a semi-presidential republic and a member of the United Nations. About half the population is Mossi, whose kingdom is led by the Mogho Naba, whose court is in Ouagadougou. There are more than 60 indigenous languages, and Mooré is spoken by more than half the population. Most people are Muslim, with Christian and animist minorities. Literature rests on oral tradition, and Ouagadougou hosts the International Art and Craft Fair, one of the most important African handicraft fairs.
